entities.name: Étienne Jacques Joseph Alexandre Macdonald
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Étienne Jacques-Joseph-Alexandre Macdonald, born in Sedan, France, on November 17, 1765, rose from a humble background to become one of Napoleon Bonaparte's most trusted and enduring military commanders, eventually earning the title Marshal of the Empire and 1st duc de Tarente. His career, spanning the turbulent French Revolutionary Wars and the Napoleonic Wars, exemplifies the meritocratic opportunities offered by the First French Empire and the complex loyalties demanded during a period of profound European upheaval. Macdonald's strategic acumen and steadfastness in battle, particularly his daring Alpine crossing during the War of the Second Coalition and his pivotal role at Wagram, cemented his place as a significant figure in early 19th-century military history.

Macdonald's military prowess first shone during the Flanders Campaign (1792-1795), where he distinguished himself at the Battle of Tourcoing. His most audacious early feat was the winter crossing of the Splügen Pass in December 1800, leading the Army of Grisons through treacherous Alpine conditions to outflank Austrian forces in Italy, a logistical and tactical masterstroke often compared to Napoleon's own crossing of the Great St Bernard. Despite a period of disfavor under Napoleon due to his association with General Moreau, Macdonald was recalled to service in 1809. His courageous leadership at the Battle of Wagram (July 5-6, 1809), where his corps formed the crucial central attack, earned him his Marshal's baton on the battlefield itself. He subsequently commanded the X Corps during the Russian Campaign of 1812, covering the northern flank, and fought valiantly during the 1813 German Campaign, notably at Lützen and Leipzig.
